Hi @carlosparadis,

> One thing we have as "domain advantage" over quanteda and igraph is that Kaiaulu is not a generalist tool for any text document or graph. Kaiaulu primarily abstracts systems and data used in software development (source code, version constrol systems, issue trackers, etc).

Regarding the domain advantage point, this was actually one of the bigger things I took away from the library research. igraph and NetworkX are powerful, but they treat every graph the same way. Kaiaulu knows what its nodes and edges actually mean because the software context is built into the API. The type columns, the named edge types, the distinction between authored and changed and modified edges in the gitlog transform are not things a user has to figure out because the function names and structure already tell them. A general graph library can never do that.

On the reply class idea, I think it connects directly to what we have been doing in graph.R. Right now, `transform_reply_to_bipartite_network` takes whatever is passed and turns it into a graph, losing where the data came from. If there was a reply class that any comment source could be converted into, then everything downstream, like the sentiment work @splimon is doing and the engagement metrics @usradam needs, could just use that class without caring if the data came from GitHub, JIRA, Bugzilla, or a mailing list. That is the same idea behind the S3 dispatch setup for graphs. The function figures out what to do based on what you pass it.

Between the two approaches, expanding the node and edgelist labels is the better option. Kaiaulu already has separate transform functions per data source, so that separation exists where it makes sense. The goal for future functions built on top of the reply object, like the engagement metrics @usradam is working on, is that they should not need to know where the data came from to do their job. If the source is just a column in the reply object, one function works on all reply objects regardless of platform. The column is there in case someone needs to filter by it later; it is ignored if they do not. Baking the source into the class type itself would mean that every future function needs a separate method for each data source, even when the logic is identical, which is exactly the kind of unnecessary complexity we want to avoid.

On the four additional tools:

**Codeface** stores everything in a MySQL database and runs from the command line with no library API. Any analysis means querying MySQL directly or using a Shiny web app. It has not been maintained since 2022. The big takeaway is that a heavy setup creates a barrier. Having to install Vagrant, MySQL, and a web server just to run an analysis is a lot, and Kaiaulu avoids all of that by keeping things in memory.

**SmartSHARK** pushes separation of concerns the furthest out of all of these tools. Each data source is its own separate command-line tool, and they all write into a shared MongoDB database using a shared data format called pycoSHARK. The way SmartSHARK splits things by data source at the repo level is basically what Kaiaulu does at the file level with R/jira.R, R/github.R, and so on. It shows that the separation is the right call. It also shows what happens when you take it too far. Setting up a full SmartSHARK environment means deploying MongoDB, a Django web server, a background worker, and configuring every plugin on its own, which is way more than most researchers want to deal with.

**PyDriller** is a Python library that gives you a clean API for reading Git repositories. You create a Repository object, iterate over commits, and each commit gives you file changes, diffs, blame data, and complexity numbers. There is no command-line tool, and nothing gets saved to disk. The API is simple and easy to use. The downside is that every time you run an analysis, it has to re-read the whole repository, which is slow for big projects. Compared to Kaiaulu wrapping Perceval as a command-line tool, PyDriller shows what it looks like to build a proper library for Git data. Kaiaulu goes through Perceval, which adds a step, but it covers a lot more data sources than just Git.

**Perceval** supports over 40 different data sources, including Git, GitHub, Jira, Bugzilla, mailing lists, and CI systems. It outputs one JSON object per item and streams it to the console. Kaiaulu uses it as a command-line dependency for parse_gitlog, so Kaiaulu runs the perceval program and reads its output rather than using it as a library. Perceval choosing to be a command-line tool instead of a library is the opposite of what PyDriller does. For Kaiaulu, this means the Git data collection part is stable and does not need to be maintained, but it also means it cannot be changed from within R. It is a clean split between collecting data and analyzing it, at the cost of needing Perceval installed.

Hi @carlosparadis,

Here are the changes I made to standardize the remaining pipelines (Understand, GitHub, Jira, Mail):

Found in my [commit](https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/pull/375/changes/9fe3f6717225c7740383ed49ff135f1d998b980c)

## Understand and Reply Pipeline Standardization

### Understand Pipeline

The understand pipeline was updated to follow the same four-stage pattern used by the gitlog and depends pipelines. The `transform_understand_dependencies_to_network` function in `src.R` was rewritten to build an explicit nodes table and an explicit edgelist table before passing them to `model_directed_graph`. Previously, the function returned a plain list with no class, which meant graph export functions like `graph_to_dsmj` could not dispatch on it. Now it returns a `directed_graph` object like the rest of the pipeline.

The vignette `understand_showcase.Rmd` was also updated. The calls to `igraph::graph_from_data_frame` were referencing the old keys `node_list` and `edge_list`. These were corrected to `nodes` and `edgelist` to match the standardized graph object structure.

### Reply Pipeline

The `transform_reply_to_bipartite_network` function in `reply.R` was updated to use `model_bipartite_graph` with an explicit nodes table and edgelist table. This corrects the return type so that downstream functions like `bipartite_graph_projection` can dispatch on it properly. The function covers the GitHub, Jira, and mbox pipelines since none of those have their own transform functions, and all route through this one.

A `source` parameter was also added to the function. It defaults to `NA_character_` and gets stored as a column in both the nodes table and the edgelist. This lets callers label where their data came from without forcing downstream functions to care about it. Functions like the engagement metrics being worked on can read all reply objects the same way, regardless of platform, and filter by source only if they need to.

### Question: Source Detection at the Parse Stage

Right now, the caller has to pass the source label manually when calling `transform_reply_to_bipartite_network`. The alternative is to have each parser add the source column automatically. `parse_mbox` would set `source = "mbox"`, `parse_jira_replies` would set `source = "jira"`, and `parse_github_replies` would set `source = "github"`. By the time the data reaches the transform function, it would already carry its origin, so no parameter would be needed.

The question is whether updating the three parsers to add a source column is the right move, or whether leaving it as a caller-supplied parameter is preferred.

The notebook section has been added, and descriptions of the class system and projections/exports are below.

## The class system

Every graph object in Kaiaulu is a named list with two entries, `nodes` and `edgelist`, with an S3 class assigned by the constructor. The four graph types are:

`directed_graph` — produced by `model_directed_graph(nodes, edgelist)`. Used for file-to-file dependency networks, function-to-function call networks, and the output of projections. Nodes have `name` and optionally `type` and `color`. Edgelist has `from`, `to`, and `weight`.

`bipartite_graph` — produced by `model_bipartite_graph(nodes, edgelist)`. Used for two-type networks such as author-file, commit-file, and author-thread. Nodes have `name`, `type` (boolean: TRUE for one side, FALSE for the other), and `color`. Edgelist has `from`, `to`, and `weight`.

`heterogeneous_graph` — produced by `model_heterogeneous_graph(nodes, edgelist)`. Used for multi-type networks such as author-commit-file. Nodes have `name`, `type` (string label like "author", "commit", "file"), and `color`. Edgelist has `from`, `to`, `weight`, `type` (string edge type like "authored" or "changed"), and `color`.

`undirected_graph` — produced by `model_undirected_graph(nodes, edgelist)`. Used for symmetric networks such as co-authorship or co-change. Same schema as `directed_graph`, but the class signals that edges have no meaningful direction.

All four constructors take only `nodes` and `edgelist` as arguments. The transform function is responsible for building those tables before calling the constructor. The constructor only wraps them and assigns the class.

## Scope of dependent functions

The transforms feed into three categories of downstream functions, all of which use S3 dispatch on the graph class.

**Projections** — `bipartite_graph_projection` and `temporal_graph_projection` both have methods for `bipartite_graph` and `heterogeneous_graph`. Both return a `directed_graph`. These are not being refactored in this PR beyond the S3 consistency fixes already made to the generic signatures. They still work because every transform that feeds them now returns a properly typed `bipartite_graph` or `heterogeneous_graph`, rather than an untyped list.

**Exports** — `graph_to_dsmj` has methods for all four graph types and dispatches correctly. The `transform_dependencies_to_sdsmj`, `transform_gitlog_to_hdsmj`, and `transform_temporal_gitlog_to_adsmj` functions all route through this. No changes were needed to the export logic itself.

**Clustering** — `community_oslom` takes a graph object and accesses `graph[["edgelist"]]` directly, reading the `from`, `to`, and `weight` columns. Since those are the standardized column names used by all graph types, `community_oslom` is already compatible with the standardized graph objects and does not need changes.

**Smells and motifs** — Functions in `smells.R` and `motif.R` consume projected `directed_graph` objects. They operate on the `edgelist` and `nodes` keys of the graph list. Since those keys are consistent across all graph types, these functions should continue to work without changes.

The notebooks listed in the issue description cover all of these downstream uses.

# 3/25 Meeting Notes

## Graph Constructors and Class System

The current graph constructors in `graph.R` give us `directed_graph`, `undirected_graph`, `bipartite_graph`, and `heterogeneous_graph`. The sponsor raised a key distinction: bipartite and heterogeneous graphs can themselves be directed or undirected, so the current class names conflate graph modality with directionality. These are separate concepts that need to be handled separately.

`heterogeneous_graph` should be renamed to `multimodal` to better reflect what it represents.

For directionality, two approaches to consider: adding it as a parameter to the constructors, or duplicating the constructors for each direction. Need to look at how Gaphor handles this in its GUI to inform the decision.

We have 3-modal type graphs that need directionality support.

## Directionality

Direction can be expressed either by column name convention or by content in the edgelist. Need to decide which approach to standardize on. igraph should be examined to see whether it cares about direction and weighting during graph projections.

Consider three directionality types: directed, undirected, and bidirected.

## Projections

Projections are not fully resolved yet. A bipartite projection removes one of the modes to produce a unimodal graph. After that, weighting on edges is a separate choice. When performing a bipartite projection it requires either/or on the node type being kept.

A `superset_bipartite_from_multimodal` convenience function should be added that separates bipartite graphs from a multimodal graph so they can be used for projections. The existing projection logic should remain the same.

When looking at the gitlog notebook, the co-change network is an example worth examining in terms of uni/bi/multimodal and directed/undirected/bidirected distinctions.

Ensure that the logic remains the same on existing projections while making these changes.

## Clustering

Clustering determines what grouping something belongs to. Clustering of graphs determines if data is connected. The distinction between graph type and directionality is important for clustering. Using information about direction and weighting is important in clustering.

## Notebooks and Convenience Functions

A strongly connected graph convenience function should be added to the reply notebook, similar to what is shown at the reply communication showcase. Examine the motif analysis notebook.

Triangle motif: 2 people and 1 file, where 2 people communicated and 1 person changed the file.

Social smell: captures collaboration without communication.

Square motif: 2 people changing 2 files that depend on each other.

## Exports

DSM export via `graph_to_dsmj` is good because it is useful for Rick's research. dv8 exporters are also relevant to keep in scope.

## Next Steps

- Rename `heterogeneous_graph` to `multimodal` across the codebase
- Look at Gaphor to determine how to represent graph directionality in the class system
- Look at igraph to see if it cares about direction and weighting during graph projections
- Decide whether directionality should be a parameter on the constructors or require separate constructors for directed and undirected variants
- Consider uni/bi/multimodal and directed/undirected/bidirected distinctions when examining the co-change network in the gitlog notebook
- Determine whether direction is expressed by column name convention or by content in the edgelist

- Ensure existing projection logic is preserved through any refactoring
- Add strongly connected graph convenience function to the reply notebook similar to the example at the reply communication showcase
- Examine the motif analysis notebook with the triangle, social smell, and square motifs in mind
- Verify dv8 and DSM exporters work correctly with any graph class changes
- Consider weighted/unweighted as a separate dimension alongside modality and directionality
